question: Which target functions are provably inaccessible to polynomial-time noisy gradient training because symmetries of the data, architecture, and initialization prevent the learner from acquiring target-specific alignment?

key_findings.claim: Equivariance of the complete gradient-training algorithm yields a general lower bound controlled by the target's alignment with its orbit under the symmetry group.
key_findings.evidence: The authors define G-equivariant training rather than only G-equivariant architectures, formalize G-alignment as the largest average squared correlation of an orbit-transformed target with a test function, and show that polynomially bounded noisy clipped population-gradient descent cannot weak-learn targets whose alignment is negligible under a G-invariant input distribution.

key_findings.claim: For standard fully connected networks, efficient weak learnability on the Boolean hypercube or unit sphere is characterized by nonnegligible low-complexity spectral content, and extra depth does not enlarge this weakly learnable class.
key_findings.evidence: Permutation, signed-permutation, or rotation symmetry follows from common i.i.d., symmetric, or Gaussian initializations. The resulting lower bounds are matched by specially initialized two-layer constructions when the target has a polynomially large Fourier coefficient of bounded or co-bounded degree on the hypercube, or a polynomially large bounded-degree spherical-harmonic component on the sphere.

anchors.section: Fully connected networks on the hypercube

key_findings.claim: The symmetry argument extends the merged-staircase obstruction for latent sparse functions beyond the mean-field parameterization.
key_findings.evidence: For permutation-equivariant noisy gradient descent, a target that first introduces an interaction of order l+1 without a chain of lower-order detectable interactions requires superlinear-in-dimension resources; the proof converts missing staircase structure into small orbit alignment rather than analyzing a particular mean-field trajectory.

key_findings.claim: Even stochastic gradient training can be conditionally hard: under a learning-parity-with-Gaussian-noise assumption, a standard symmetrically initialized fully connected learner cannot efficiently recover a modular target from noisy samples.
key_findings.evidence: A reduction exploits sign-flip equivariance and embeds a noisy parity instance into learning a sum-modulo-eight target. If the stated fully connected SGD learner succeeded in polynomial resources, it would violate the assumed cryptographic hardness of the source problem.

method.core_idea: Lift symmetries from a network and its initialization to the entire randomized training algorithm, then turn a target's small correlation with its group orbit into a resource lower bound for noisy gradient learning.
method.mechanism: The proof couples runs on symmetry-transformed targets, averages their gradient signals over the group, and bounds expected progress using G-alignment. Fourier analysis on the hypercube and spherical harmonics on the sphere evaluate that alignment; permutation orbits expose staircase obstructions; a separate reduction transfers a noisy-parity hardness assumption to SGD.
assumptions: The input distribution is invariant under the chosen group action and the full training procedure is equivariant in distribution.
Population-gradient updates are clipped and perturbed by isotropic Gaussian noise, with step size, number of steps, clipping radius, model size, and inverse noise bounded polynomially.
Weak learning means obtaining a nonnegligible correlation advantage, not arbitrary-accuracy regression or finite-sample benchmark performance.
The SGD hardness result is conditional on the stated learning-parity-with-Gaussian-noise cryptographic assumption.
Matching upper bounds may use deliberately target-compatible two-layer initializations rather than the standard symmetric initialization ruled out by the lower bounds.

techniques.role: Tracks symmetry through initialization, gradient computation, clipping, and injected noise.
Quantifies the maximum learnable signal remaining after averaging a target over a symmetry orbit.
Turns abstract alignment into explicit degree conditions on the hypercube and sphere.
Relates missing hierarchical interactions in sparse targets to costly permutation orbits.
Converts a hypothetical efficient SGD learner into an algorithm for noisy parity.

evaluations.setting: Boolean targets under uniform hypercube inputs
evaluations.result: The characterization requires a polynomially detectable Fourier coefficient at bounded degree or bounded co-degree; a tailored depth-two learner achieves the positive direction.
evaluations.baseline: Arbitrary-depth fully connected networks trained by equivariant noisy gradient descent

evaluations.setting: Square-integrable targets under the uniform sphere distribution
evaluations.result: Efficient weak learning is equivalent, under the theorem's resource model, to a nonnegligible projection onto a bounded-degree spherical-harmonic subspace.
Violating the l-merged-staircase hierarchy induces a dimension-dependent lower bound, extending the earlier mean-field necessity result to a broad permutation-equivariant noisy-GD class.

evaluations.setting: Noisy modular target under an LPGN assumption
evaluations.result: An efficient standard fully connected SGD learner would break the assumed noisy-parity problem, establishing conditional non-learnability.

limitations: The central unconditional bounds concern deliberately noisy clipped population gradient descent, not every optimizer or ordinary finite-batch training recipe.
Exact group invariance is strong; natural data distributions are generally only approximately symmetric, and the paper leaves robust approximate-invariance extensions open.
The analysis targets weak correlation and stylized distributions rather than test accuracy, representation learning, or scaling behavior on realistic tasks.
Positive results rely on specially engineered initial features, so they characterize possibility more than what off-the-shelf initialization discovers.
The SGD modular-function separation is cryptographic and therefore conditional, not an unconditional optimization lower bound.
failure_modes: Interpreting architectural universality as trainability ignores the symmetry-induced absence of gradient signal identified here.
A small but practically important symmetry-breaking bias in data, initialization, positional features, or optimization can invalidate an exact equivariance lower bound.
Removing artificial gradient noise may destroy the proof while leaving the empirical training process either easy or hard for unrelated reasons.
A target with a detectable low-degree component can be weakly learned even if its main high-degree structure remains inaccessible, so weak success need not mean task solution.
Target-aware initialization can evade a lower bound but simply move prior knowledge into model design.
reusable_insights: State symmetry claims at the level of the data-training algorithm pair, not architecture alone.
Before running large experiments, decompose a target under the optimizer's symmetry group and measure whether any polynomially visible component exists.
Distinguish an expressivity theorem from a trainability theorem and a weak-correlation guarantee from full prediction performance.
Treat initialization and positional or feature asymmetries as information channels that can make an otherwise invisible target learnable.
Use reductions and group alignment to obtain optimizer-agnostic lower bounds without solving the full nonlinear trajectory.
open_questions: How does the master bound degrade under quantitatively approximate data or training equivariance?
Can comparable unconditional limits be proved for noiseless finite-batch SGD, momentum, Adam, or adaptive preconditioning?
Which naturally occurring tasks have small symmetry alignment after realistic augmentation and positional encoding?
Can training dynamically break a symmetry before acquiring target signal, and what minimum asymmetry is needed?
Is there a clean spectral characterization of strong rather than weak learnability for common network-optimizer pairs?

competitive_landscape.title: Poly-time universality and limitations of deep learning
competitive_landscape.relationship: foundational polynomial-time universality and non-universality framework
competitive_landscape.difference: Abbe and Sandon use cross-predictability to separate universal small-batch SGD from noisy large-batch GD across function distributions; this paper derives target-specific limitations from training equivariance and group alignment and adds sharper hypercube, sphere, and staircase characterizations.

competitive_landscape.title: An initial alignment between neural network and target is needed for gradient descent to learn
competitive_landscape.difference: Initial Alignment measures correlation between a randomly initialized network and Boolean target; the present work generalizes the mechanism to arbitrary equivariant training algorithms and a group-orbit alignment independent of one architecture's initial outputs.

competitive_landscape.title: The merged-staircase property: a necessary and nearly sufficient condition for SGD learning of sparse functions on two-layer neural networks
competitive_landscape.difference: The merged-staircase paper proves a near characterization for two-layer mean-field SGD; this paper recovers a necessity hierarchy for a much wider equivariant noisy-gradient class but does not inherit the same constructive sufficiency in that generality.

competitive_landscape.title: On the Power of Differentiable Learning versus PAC and SQ Learning
competitive_landscape.relationship: alternative computational characterization of gradient learning
competitive_landscape.difference: That work characterizes when gradient precision and batch size make differentiable learning equivalent to SQ or powerful enough to simulate PAC learning; the symmetry paper instead fixes a noisy-gradient resource model and identifies which targets its invariant signal cannot distinguish.

novelty_assessment: Reviewer inference: the key advance is a modular symmetry-to-hardness theorem for the entire randomized training procedure, followed by unusually sharp spectral applications. It subsumes the intuition of initial alignment and extends the merged-staircase necessity beyond one parameterization. Its reach should not be overstated: exact invariance, explicit injected noise, weak learning, and a conditional cryptographic component leave a substantial gap to ordinary large-model SGD on natural data.
reviewer_notes: All 36 extracted pages were reviewed, including definitions and the master theorem, hypercube and sphere corollaries, matching two-layer constructions, merged-staircase analysis, the LPGN reduction, and appendices. No empirical benchmark is presented; the evaluation entries above are theorem settings. Primary competing arXiv records were checked on 2026-08-23, and the lower-bound scope is stated narrowly to avoid treating noisy clipped population GD as synonymous with all deep learning.
